facts.name: Garden Verbena
facts.color: Purple, lilac-blue, pink, red or white clusters (purple shown)
facts.notes: Low, spreading mats covered in round clusters of small flowers from planting until frost; butterflies and hummingbirds visit. An annual here: plant after the last frost in late May. Superbena types bloom without deadheading; trim the stem tips by about a fifth in midsummer for a fuller plant. Not the same plant as our native Blue Vervain.

sources.title: English Gardens (Metro Detroit garden centers): Superbena Large Lilac Blue Verbena
sources.note: Sold at English Gardens as an annual: about 12 inches tall, spreading 3 ft, planted about 28 inches apart.

sources.title: Illinois Extension: Garden Verbena
sources.note: Annual for sunny, dry sites, 6 to 14 inches tall; blooms May to October in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil. Attracts butterflies. Can be cut back to shape.

sources.title: Proven Winners: Superbena Peachy Keen verbena
sources.note: Superbena flowers nonstop from planting to frost. For a fuller plant, trim up to 20% off the stem ends midseason. In heavy, soggy soil, grow it in a pot.

sources.title: Rutgers NJAES: Landscape Plants Rated by Deer Resistance (printable list)
sources.note: Annuals: calendula and strawflower are rated A (rarely damaged); California poppy, verbena and zinnia B (seldom severely damaged); cosmos C (occasionally severely damaged).

sources.title: ASPCA: Lemon Verbena
sources.note: ASPCA lists lemon verbena (Aloysia, a different plant) as toxic; garden verbena isn't on its lists.

companions.why: Verbena adds a delicate touch that complements zinnias.
